items.title: Half-life is a probability, not a clock
items.claim: A radioactive nucleus has a half-life of 5730 years. People imagine each atom has a 5730-year fuse. In fact each atom's decay is fundamentally random — no ageing, no internal clock.
items.prompt: If you watch a single carbon-14 nucleus for 5730 years, what is the chance it decays in the next year?

options.text: Almost 100 percent — it's used up its half-life
About 1 in 8267 — exactly the same as a freshly made C-14 nucleus

items.reveal:
The probability of decay per unit time (decay constant lambda) is fixed for a given isotope. A nucleus 'remembers' nothing about how long it has existed. For C-14, lambda equals ln 2 over 5730 years, so per year the decay chance is about 1 part in 8267 — for every individual nucleus, every year.

Half-life emerges from large populations of identical-but-independent random events. With one nucleus there is no half-life — only a probability distribution. With Avogadro's number of nuclei the law of large numbers makes the exponential decay law deterministic.

This is fundamentally different from human ageing or battery discharge — those have internal state that changes with time.
items.why: Half-life is intuitively pictured as countdown. It's actually a statistical property of populations of memoryless processes.

items.title: A catalyst can be a product
items.claim: Autocatalytic reactions speed up as they proceed. The classic example: the oxidation of oxalic acid by permanganate. Manganese(II) ions, a product, catalyse the very reaction that makes them.
items.prompt: What does the rate-time curve look like for an autocatalytic reaction?

options.text: A constant rate from start to finish
S-shaped: slow start, accelerating middle, then slowing again as reactants run out
A straight line decreasing to zero
A spike at the start, then decay

items.reveal_title: Sigmoidal kinetics — a chemical population explosion
items.reveal:
At the start there is little catalyst, so the rate is slow. As Mn2+ builds up, rate accelerates. Eventually permanganate runs out and the rate falls. The curve is identical in shape to bacterial growth, viral epidemics or chain reactions — all are autocatalytic.

Life itself may be a form of autocatalysis: replication makes more replicators. Some prebiotic chemistry research focuses on finding the first autocatalytic networks that could bootstrap life on Earth.
items.why: Most introductory examples show monotonic rates. Autocatalysis breaks the simple 'rate falls as reactants decrease' story.

items.title: Aluminium 'wants' to react but doesn't
items.claim: Aluminium has a standard electrode potential of minus 1.66 V — more reactive than zinc or iron. It should fizz in water and burn in air. Yet aluminium aircraft, foil and cans sit happily for years.
items.prompt: Why doesn't aluminium corrode in air?

options.text: Pure aluminium does not react with oxygen
Aluminium instantly forms a coherent, impermeable 4 nanometre oxide layer (Al2O3) that protects the metal underneath
The factory coats aluminium with plastic before sale
Standard electrode potentials are unreliable for s and p block metals

items.reveal_title: Thermodynamics screams react! — but a passivation layer locks the door
items.reveal:
Aluminium oxide forms in milliseconds when fresh aluminium meets oxygen. Unlike iron oxide (rust), Al2O3 has almost the same molar volume as the underlying metal, so it forms a tight, adherent film. Oxygen can't reach the metal beneath, and the reaction effectively stops.

Remove the oxide (scratch it, dissolve it in alkali, or amalgamate the surface with mercury), and aluminium reacts violently. This is why aluminium powder + iron oxide (thermite) is dangerous, and why aluminium ships are vulnerable to mercury contamination.
items.why: Reactivity series is about thermodynamic tendency. Kinetics — including passivation — decides whether the reaction is observable.
